params.question: What does the video identify as the PRIMARY reason for India's wide interstate variation in under-5 mortality?

answers.text: Shortage of trained medical professionals at the national level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The video clarifies that the gap is not about overall resource scarcity. NFHS-5 shows a fourfold mortality difference between Kerala and UP, driven by differences in how resources are planned, allocated, and managed.

answers.text: Differences in climate and disease ecology across states

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Climate affects disease patterns, but the video attributes the interstate gap to unequal planning, investment, and programme quality — not ecological differences.

answers.text: Unequal planning, investment, and programme quality across states

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The video states this disparity is 'driven by unequal investment, infrastructure, and programme quality.' Without deliberate planning, resources flow toward visible urban hospitals while rural sub-centres stay understaffed.

answers.text: Lack of advanced medical technology in poorer states

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: India runs nuclear reactors and space missions — the issue is not technological capacity. The video emphasises that the gap is a planning failure: resources exist but are not systematically directed where they are needed most.

overallFeedback.feedback: The video shows that India has the resources but distributes them unevenly. NFHS-5 data reveals a fourfold mortality gap between states, driven by differences in planning, investment, and programme quality — not by resource scarcity or climate.
Exactly right. India's health outcome disparities reflect planning and investment failures rather than absolute resource shortages — the central argument for why systematic health planning matters.

interactions.label: A newly appointed District Health Officer discovers that only 40% of sub-centres

params.question: A newly appointed District Health Officer discovers that only 40% of sub-centres in her district have adequate drug supplies. Applying the planning cycle as demonstrated in the NHM, what should be her FIRST step?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ordering drugs is an implementation step (phase 4). Without first understanding why supplies are inadequate — whether from ordering delays, storage issues, or distribution failures — the same problem will recur.

answers.text: Conduct a situation analysis of the supply chain gaps

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The planning cycle begins with situation analysis — examining current conditions, identifying specific gaps, and understanding root causes. The NHM itself started by analysing infrastructure and staffing data before designing any intervention.

answers.text: Formulate a comprehensive five-year drug supply plan

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Plan formulation is the third phase. Without first analysing the specific causes of the stockout (situation analysis) and ranking problems by severity and feasibility (priority setting), the plan may address the wrong issue.

answers.text: Evaluate the performance of existing sub-centre staff

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Evaluation is the fifth phase of the planning cycle, used to assess outcomes of an existing programme. A new officer confronting a gap should begin with situation analysis to understand the problem's root causes.

overallFeedback.feedback: The planning cycle's first phase is situation analysis — identifying what's wrong and why. The NHM started by examining data on staffing, drug supply, and mortality before setting priorities or designing programmes.
Well done. Just as the NHM began with data from the Bulletin of Rural Health Statistics to expose staffing and supply gaps, any planning effort must start with a thorough situation analysis.

interactions.label: What is the KEY distinction between cost-effectiveness analysis and cost-benefit

params.question: What is the KEY distinction between cost-effectiveness analysis and cost-benefit analysis in health programme evaluation?

answers.text: CEA is used for preventive programmes; CBA is used for curative programmes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The distinction is not about programme type. Both tools can evaluate any programme. CEA measures outcomes in health units (e.g., DALYs averted); CBA converts all outcomes to monetary terms to assess overall economic worth.

answers.text: CEA measures outcomes in health units; CBA converts all outcomes into monetary terms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. CEA compares cost per health outcome (e.g., cost per DALY averted), allowing efficiency comparisons within one metric. CBA monetises both costs and benefits, answering whether a programme is economically worth doing at all — crucial for large infrastructure decisions.

answers.text: CEA includes quality-of-life adjustments; CBA measures only survival

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Quality-of-life adjustment is the hallmark of cost-utility analysis (CUA), which uses QALYs. CEA uses natural health units without quality weighting; CBA monetises all outcomes. Neither is defined by quality-of-life adjustment.

answers.text: CEA is used at the national level; CBA is used at the district level

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both methods can be applied at any administrative level. The real distinction lies in what they measure: CEA uses health units for efficiency comparison, while CBA converts everything to money to determine net economic value.

overallFeedback.feedback: The core distinction: CEA measures outcomes in natural health units (DALYs averted, cases cured) for efficiency comparisons, while CBA converts all benefits to money to determine whether a programme's total economic value exceeds its cost.

Exactly. CEA asks 'which programme gives more health per rupee?' while CBA asks 'is this programme worth doing at all?' — two fundamentally different questions requiring different measurement approaches.

interactions.label: India has completed its epidemiological transition and now faces primarily a non

params.question: India has completed its epidemiological transition and now faces primarily a non-communicable disease burden.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: India has not completed its epidemiological transition. Unlike high-income countries where NCDs dominate, India faces a triple burden — communicable diseases persist, non-communicable diseases are rising, and injuries contribute significantly. This unique challenge demands health planning that addresses all three domains concurrently.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. India has NOT completed its epidemiological transition. It faces a triple burden: communicable diseases (TB, malaria) persist, non-communicable diseases (heart disease, diabetes) are rising sharply, and injuries add a third dimension. Health planning must address all three simultaneously.

interactions.label: A 35-year-old vegetable vendor in an urban market earns above the PM-JAY income

params.question: A 35-year-old vegetable vendor in an urban market earns above the PM-JAY income threshold but has no employer-sponsored health insurance. Under the current Ayushman Bharat framework, which situation BEST describes this person's coverage?

answers.text: Fully covered by both Health and Wellness Centre services and PM-JAY hospitalisation benefit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PM-JAY targets the poorest 40% of households (around 50 crore people). An informal worker earning above this threshold does not qualify for PM-JAY's ₹5 lakh cashless hospital cover, though they can access HWC primary care.

answers.text: Covered for primary care at HWCs but unprotected against catastrophic hospital expenses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This person is part of the 'missing middle' — they can access the 12 categories of primary care at Health and Wellness Centres, but earn too much for PM-JAY eligibility and lack formal employer insurance, leaving them exposed to ruinous out-of-pocket hospital costs.

answers.text: Automatically enrolled in the state government's insurance scheme as a fallback

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no automatic fallback enrolment for informal workers above the PM-JAY threshold. The video identifies this group as the 'missing middle' — a major gap where informal workers remain uncovered for catastrophic hospitalisation costs.

answers.text: Ineligible for any Ayushman Bharat services because they are not below the poverty line

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Health and Wellness Centres provide comprehensive primary care to all, not only BPL populations. The gap is specifically in hospital cover: this person can use HWCs but falls outside PM-JAY's cashless hospitalisation benefit.

overallFeedback.feedback: This person represents the 'missing middle.' They can access HWC primary care services, but earn too much for PM-JAY's cashless hospital cover and have no employer insurance — leaving catastrophic hospitalisation costs uncovered.
Well identified. The 'missing middle' — informal workers who earn above PM-JAY thresholds but lack formal insurance — is a recognised gap in Ayushman Bharat's universal health coverage design.
